articles.title: Who
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Walkers who know Healey Dell will recognise the narrow cleft of the Spodden called the Thrutch and the little rock alcove that has long been known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The “Healey Dwarf” is the best‑known supernatural figure attached to that place: in local telling a tiny, ginger‑bearded person — sometimes imagined as a stone sentinel in the river — who belongs among the fairies. But the dwarf, like other elements of the Dell’s story‑map, belongs to folklore rather than to the archive of verifiable events.

The oldest printed witness for the tale that survives in wide circulation is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire. Roby collected and published local romances and legends in the early nineteenth century (his Lancashire volumes first appeared in 1829–31), and his chapter often cited as “The Fairies’ Chapel” gathers the characters and episodes — a cavern‑like cleft, a miller, a Fairy Queen and a small figure associated with the place — that later writers repeated and reshaped. Roby’s work is a primary source for the story as it was told in his era, but it must be read as a collector’s and storyteller’s account: it records oral tradition and contemporary retelling rather than offering documentary proof of supernatural events.

Later Victorian and local writers elaborated Roby’s material. A small book published in 1882, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, gives a fully dramatised and poetical version in which a character called Healey (often pictured with a ginger beard in these retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later accounts are useful for tracking how the dwarf’s image — costume, beard and behaviour — became fixed in local imagination, but they are literary treatments rather than independent contemporary testimonies.

On the ground today the concrete facts are straightforward and separate from the stories. Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology — mill remains, waterfalls and the Victorian viaduct — and a heritage centre that presents the site’s history and folklore for visitors. The rock formation that inspired the name Fairies’ Chapel is a water‑worn niche; the site was altered by extreme flooding in the 1830s, and the physical features visible now are not identical to those seen by earlier visitors. Local authorities and the heritage centre present the dwarf and related tales as part of the Dell’s living folklore rather than as documented historical personages.

What we can say with confidence: the Healey Dwarf is a figure of local tradition preserved in nineteenth‑century printed collections and in later local retellings. The earliest reliable printed appearance is John Roby’s collection; later writers — including the 1882 verse volume — shaped the dwarf’s popular image. What cannot be verified from official records is any claim that a living dwarf or a supernatural guardian actually inhabited the Dell: there are no archival documents, legal records or contemporary official investigations that establish such a thing as historical fact.

If you want to explore the sources, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest widely available printed version and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material and Rochdale Borough Council’s site listings for the reserve’s geology, industrial remains and how the folklore is presented to visitors today. The story of the Healey Dwarf is best approached as local folklore — a useful lens on how people in and around Healey have imagined their landscape over two centuries — and as an example of the way place, geology and human storytelling become entangled.

Visiting the Dell remains the most direct way to meet the tradition: the rock alcove, the Thrutch, the viaduct and the heritage displays are all real; the dwarf lives in the stories people tell there.

articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Short answer: no contemporary evidence — the Robin Hood link is a nineteenth‑century folk tale layered onto a real landscape of mills, a dramatic viaduct and a flood‑scarred rock called the Fairies’ Chapel.
articles.summary: Short answer: no contemporary evidence — the Robin Hood link is a nineteenth‑century folk tale layered onto a real landscape of mills, a dramatic viaduct and a flood‑scarred rock called the Fairies’ Chapel.
articles.body:
Ask whether Robin Hood ever strode through Healey Dell and the practical answer is immediate: there is no archival or archaeological evidence that the historical figure known as Robin Hood — or a medieval outlaw called Robert of Huntingdon — ever visited the Dell. What people now call the Dell’s Robin Hood story belongs to the region’s printed and oral folklore, first collected and popularised in the nineteenth century and kept alive by later guidebooks and the Heritage Centre.

The storyline you’ll hear on a summer visit is recognisably Victorian. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first issued 1829–31) records a long local romance set around the Thrutch — the narrow, water‑cut cleft in the Spodden known to locals — that mixes a miller, a prophetic “Fairy Queen”, witches, a little “Healey Dwarf” and a tale about an uncle’s ring that sends a character called Robert towards his fate. Later nineteenth‑century writers dramatised the material further (an 1882 verse book by R. Standring, for example). The Healey Dell Heritage Centre and modern local guides retell that same cluster of stories, and they explicitly treat them as folklore rather than as documentary history.

Those literary origins matter. Roby and his successors were collectors and storytellers: their value to historians is as records of what people told and believed in their times, not as court rolls, land deeds or eyewitness reports that would prove a historical visit. The University of Manchester’s desk‑based archaeological assessment of the Dell (carried out for Rochdale council) shows the kinds of primary sources available for the area — county SMRs, manuscript and printed maps, records held at the Lancashire Record Office and the John Rylands Library — and the study’s focus is the Dell’s industrial remains, mines and mills. Those archival and archaeological records document mills, transport features and later industry; they do not contain contemporary records that place Robin Hood, or any medieval outlaw by that name, at Healey Dell.

The landscape facts are straightforward and authoritative. Healey Dell is a protected local nature reserve with substantial industrial archaeology: mill sites, a disused 1800s railway line and a striking Victorian viaduct. The viaduct that dominates the gorge was built in 1869–70 and is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England (Historic England list entry 1317784). The feature known as the Fairies’ Chapel — a rock alcove at the base of the Thrutch whose eroded seats and pulpit once fired imaginations — was further altered by a violent storm and flood on 4 July 1838, which contemporary reports and later local guides record as seriously damaging bridges, mills and the chapel features.

So where did the Robin Hood element come from? The short version: storytelling practice. Roby and later local writers folded together regional motifs common in English folklore — prophetic fairy queens, boggarts or dwarfs, witches turned to stone, and the medieval outlaw hero of popular ballads — to create a compelling local romance. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre uses those tales in family trails and displays because they are part of the Dell’s cultural history; the centre does not present them as verified historical events.

If you want to decide for yourself: read Roby (his Traditions of Lancashire is online), then walk the marked trails from the Heritage Centre and stand beneath the viaduct. You will leave with two clear truths: the Dell is a well‑documented piece of industrial and natural heritage, and it is also a place where landscape and imagination have met for centuries. Treat the Robin Hood story as a local tradition worth enjoying; treat claims of an actual historical visit with healthy scepticism unless someone produces a dated document or archaeological find to prove it.

Practical details: Healey Dell is managed as a visitor site by Rochdale Borough Council (visitor information, opening times and parking are available through the council’s Healey Dell page). For the earliest printed versions of the tales, start with John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire; for the site’s industrial and archaeological record consult the University of Manchester desk assessment and the Historic England listing for the viaduct.

What remains open — and worth keeping an eye on — is how the Dell’s story is told. Local heritage bodies and the Heritage Centre choose how to present legend alongside fact; readers wanting precise documentary proof should expect to find it in archives and archaeological reports, not in Roby’s romances.

articles.title: Christ Church Healey to hold Harvest celebration and special bell-blessing service
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest service on 18 October, followed by a special afternoon service to bless the church bells with the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark.
articles.content_html:
Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest celebration on Sunday 18 October, with the church also welcoming the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark for a special service to bless its bells later the same day.

The Harvest service begins at 10am. The church is asking those attending to bring donations of non-perishable food, which will be given to the food bank.

A second service will take place at 2pm, when the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark will join the congregation for a special service to bless the bells.

The bell-blessing service will be followed by light refreshments in the church hall.

Christ Church Healey is inviting members of the local community to join both services and take part in the day's celebrations.
articles.legal_disclaimer: This article was compiled from information supplied by Christ Church Healey. Service arrangements and timings should be confirmed directly with the church if circumstances change.

articles.title: Can’t make it to church? Christ Church Healey invites community to join Sunday service online
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey is inviting people who cannot attend in person, are new to church or simply want to find out more to join its Sunday morning service online each week.
articles.content_html:
People across Healey and the wider Rochdale community who are unable to attend church in person are being warmly invited to join Christ Church's Sunday morning service online each week.

The church's weekly livestream is also open to people who may be new to church, curious about Christianity or who would simply feel more comfortable experiencing a service from home before deciding whether to attend in person.

Christ Church goes live at 9.55am every Sunday morning, allowing viewers to watch the service as it happens. Anyone who cannot watch at that time can catch up afterwards, with the service remaining available to view later.

The church said: “You are most welcome to join us for our weekly Sunday morning livestream from Christ Church. You can watch the service live as it happens, or at any time afterwards. We go live at 9.55am.”

For people who are housebound, unwell, caring for somebody, working on Sunday mornings or otherwise unable to be physically present, the livestream provides a way to remain connected with worship and the local church community.

It can also offer a gentle introduction for anyone who has never attended church before. There is no requirement to already be a member of the congregation — viewers can simply tune in from home and see what a Sunday morning at Christ Church is like.

The livestream runs each Sunday, with the broadcast beginning at 9.55am. Christ Church Healey welcomes both its existing congregation and newcomers joining online.

articles.title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?
